sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Gao et al., 2023b; Fan et al., 2024) combines choices across many pipeline stages. Our study covers eight stages that span the dominant design axes in modern RAG (Fig. 1b; full catalog in Section K): embedding, chunking, index-time enrichment, retrieval, query augmentation, reranking, context compression, and agentic quality gates. Most new techniques are proposed and evaluated one stage at time, in isolation from the surrounding pipeline, or from several representative pipelines that would test whether findings generalize (Yu et al., 2024). Adding to the complexity, RAG systems are evaluated for two goals (Saad-Falcon et al., 2024; Friel et al., 2024): retrieving the right content (NDCG@10) and producing faithful answer from it (RAGAS; Es et al., 2024). It is unclear whether isolated gains persist under composition. It is also unclear whether the same design choices optimize both retrieval quality (which documents are retrieved) and answer faithfulness (whether the answer is grounded in those documents), two goals RAG evaluation typically reports separately. We pre-declare three hypotheses. H1. Components often fail to compose: isolated gains from single-component ablations do not necessarily persist when components are combined. H2. simple RAG pipeline can be near-optimal in many settings, while more elaborate configurations tend to specialize to narrower ones. Most RAG ablations in the literature run at 5K to 50K documents, whereas the applications RAG can serve run at corpora an order of magnitude larger; H3. composition rankings shift with corpus scale, so conclusions from small-corpus benchmarks may not hold at larger scales. These interactions, and how they change with corpus scale, remain largely unquantified. Testing these hypotheses requires framework that isolates pipeline stages and supports reproducible evaluation across benchmarks. We created LASAGNA, an open-source RAG framework, to provide this (Fig. 1a, Section 3). Each stage sits behind fixed interface, so swapping one method cannot silently change the implementation at another. Adding new technique is single line of code; the framework tests it inside complete modern pipeline without reimplementing the surrounding stack. We use LASAGNA to study RAG composition with 167-configuration D-optimal design (Fedorov et al., 1972; Atkinson et al., 2007) across eight configurable stages of modern RAG pipeline  (Table 10)  , eight benchmarks  (Fig. 5)  , and corpus sizes from 5K to 200K documents, complemented by 138 non-factorial ablation configurations across 24 targeted experiments (Section F). Across the factorial, ablation suite, and scaling sweep, the central finding is that techniques that perform well separately do not consistently retain their gains inside full pipeline, and the pattern differs between retrieval and faithfulness. Retrieval gains compose sub-additively: the three largest singlecomponent improvements sum to predicted +47% NDCG@10 gain, but the composed pipeline realizes only +17% (Section D.14). Faithfulness gains compose near-additively: separately measured improvements approximately transfer to the full pipeline  (Table 47)  . Pipeline and generator also partly substitute: stronger generator helps the lightest pipeline far more than the heaviest, so heavier stack buys less when the generator is already strong (Section F.9). Three practical implications follow. First, the components that improve retrieval are not the same as those that improve faithfulness, and optimizing one metric can hurt the other. Second, the four complete RAG profiles expose Pareto tradeoff on retrieval quality, faithfulness, and response time, with no universal winner. Adding an agentic loop to strong retrieval stack yields only negligible faithfulness gain while hurting retrieval quality and latency. Across three other benchmarks at 100K200K documents, lighter pipelines retain similar measured quality at 1020 lower latency (Sections D.8 and 5). Third, corpus size shifts profile rankings: the design leading at small corpora trails by 13.7% NDCG@10 at 200K, with rank flip visible from 25K (Fig. 4a). sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Modern RAG spans layered design space with plausible interaction points at every stage (full method catalog in Section K). On retrieval, sparse baselines (BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009)) coexist with dense encoders (BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2024a), E5 (Wang et al., 2022)), learned sparse encoders (SPLADE (Formal et al., 2021)), and late-interaction models (ColBERT (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020)), fused by reciprocal-rank fusion (RRF) (Cormack et al., 2009) or learned hybrids. Reranking spans cross-encoder scorers trained on MS-MARCO (Nogueira & Cho, 2019), ensemble rerankers, and diversity-driven selection (MMR; Carbonell & Goldstein, 1998). Context compression is either token-budget aware (LLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023a)) or positional (lost-in-the-middle-aware selection (Liu et al., 2024)). Query augmentation rewrites the query before retrieval: HyDE (Gao et al., 2023a) drafts hypothetical answer, RAG-Fusion (Rackauckas, 2024) fans out multi-query variants, decomposition (Khattab et al., 2024) splits multi-hop questions into sub-questions, and step-back prompting (Zheng et al., 2024) abstracts before retrieving. Index-time processing enriches chunks before retrieval with document summaries (RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024)), contextual prefixes (Anthropic, 2024), or entity-graph indexes (GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024)). Generation-time control adds correction and gating loops around the answer model (CRAG (Yan et al., 2024), SelfRAG (Asai et al., 2024), Speculative-RAG (Wang et al., 2025)). Each of these stages has been shown to help in isolation on some benchmark, but they compose along more edges than single-component ablation can enumerate. We study how these choices combine once deployed together, and LASAGNA lets others ask compositionality questions in the same environment by registering new component and evaluating it against full modern pipeline. Table 1 positions LASAGNA against prior work that studies RAG beyond isolated components. Best-practice studies (Wang et al., 2024; Barnett et al., 2024) search greedily for strong end-to-end configurations but do not estimate interaction effects. Benchmarking libraries such as BERGEN (Rau et al., 2024) and FlashRAG (Jin et al., 2025) support composition in shared codebase but do not enforce the stage isolation that controlled interaction estimation requires, so measured differences cannot be cleanly attributed to the component being varied (a positional smoke run against both is reported in Section G.4). Automated configuration search (Kim et al., 2024) optimizes over configurations but reports only the winning setting, not the interaction structure that produced it, so the resulting guidance does not transfer when any assumption changes. Evaluation suites (Krishna et al., 2025) and domain benchmarks (Xiong et al., 2024) supply metrics and tasks but not common pipeline in which those metrics can be compared across controlled compositions. Generation-time controls (Yan et al., 2024) strengthen the agentic layer but are usually tested with retrieval fixed, leaving composition with tuned stack untested.

sections.title: 3 LASAGNA: A COMPOSITIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR RAG
sections.content: LASAGNA is an open-source framework for evaluating new RAG components inside complete modern pipeline. researcher proposing new reranker, chunker, or agentic loop today must either compare against stripped-down baseline that does not reflect modern pipeline, or reimplement the surrounding stack. The first biases the conclusion by mixing implementation differences with algorithmic ones; the second is prohibitively expensive and rarely attempted. LASAGNA provides configurable end-to-end pipeline (Fig. 1a) with fixed interface per stage that the framework enforces, so new component drops into one stage and is measured against the same surrounding stack used by every reported configuration (full code patterns in Sections H.2.2 to H.2.4). The workflow spans nine processing stages: document processing, chunking, index-time enrichment, embedding and indexing, query augmentation, retrieval, reranking, context compression, and answer generation with optional agentic verification. Every pipeline component is subclass of typed abstract base class: eight component types are supported (embedder, chunker, reranker, retriever, document_processor, query_enhancer, agentic_pipeline, and generator), each stages inputs and outputs are typed dataclass contracts, and behavioral tests check that swapping one implementation does not mutate neighboring stages state. single @registry.register("<stage>", "<name>") decorator suffices to make new component discoverable at YAML-config time. The framework ships with 53 built-in components, the 30 methods across the eight factorial dimensions (Table 10; full catalog in Section K), six vector backends (Milvus, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, pgvector, OpenSearch), and adapters for the eight benchmarks used here (five BEIR retrieval sets and three long-form QA sets; Section B.2). Five automated isolation tests (Section H.1) check that toggling one component does not silently change another, including that two sessions with opposite settings each keep their own configuration; this supports attributing the interaction estimates in Section 5 to the components we vary rather than to cross-stage leakage. new component becomes publishable comparison in three steps  (Fig. 2)  : register with decorator, declare factorial sweep in YAML, and run end-to-end to receive paired statistical test against the same surrounding stack that produced every reported number. The complete study, factorial plus 138 non-factorial ablations plus the 5K200K scaling sweep, cost approximately $5,200 in cloud compute and 310 wall-clock hours (Section A.7).

sections.content: Factorial design. The configuration space spans eight experimental dimensions, with 25 levels each (Fig. 1b, Table 10). The full factorial of 44435424 = 30,720 configurations would exceed 40,000 GPU-hours and $600,000 in LLM API costs (extrapolating from the executed 167-configuration budget of 247 GPU-hours and $5,200; Section A.7), roughly two orders of magnitude beyond our resources, so we draw 242-run D-optimal subset via Fedorov coordinate exchange (Fedorov et al., 1972), sized to keep all main effects and all 28 dimension-pair interactions estimable under our budget. Of the 242 planned runs, 167 were executed: 63 GraphRAG-enriched runs were dropped after an isolated ablation showed no measurable NDCG@10 change despite the 2 latency the enrichment added  (Table 11)  , and 12 failed on timeout limits. Design-matrix construction, aliasing diagnostics, and the identifiability audit for the pre-declared joint 28-two-way test appear in Sections A.4, A.5 and D.3. Each dimension uses simple, lowest-cost baseline; pre-registration deviations appear in Table 12. unified multi-domain corpus, two evaluation tracks. Production RAG deployments operate against heterogeneous knowledge bases where single retriever must disambiguate biomedical, financial, scientific, argumentative, and multi-hop queries from one shared vector store. Per-benchmark evaluation (the BEIR default; Thakur et al., 2021) under-tests this cross-domain distractor pressure. We therefore unify our eight evaluation benchmarks into one corpus: five BEIR sets cover retrieval (NFCorpus, Boteva et al., 2016; FiQA, Maia et al., 2018; SciFact, Wadden et al., 2020; ArguAna, Wachsmuth et al., 2018; HotpotQA, Yang et al., 2018) and three QA sets cover generation (SQuAD v2, Rajpurkar et al., 2018; MuSiQue, Trivedi et al., 2022), yielding 149 stratified queries per configuration (Sections B.1 and B.2 and Tables 15 to 17). Each configuration is evaluated on two tracks: retrieval (BEIR qrels over 5,132 documents, 93 queries) and end-to-end generation (the same corpus augmented with gold passages, 5,566 documents, 56 queries). Beyond the 167-run factorial, we additionally ran 138 non-factorial ablation configurations across 24 targeted experiments spanning rerankers, embeddings, chunkers, query augmentation, and the number of agentic verification iterations (Section F). Together with the corpus-scaling sweep (5K200K), the study records approximately 358,215 individual query evaluations, including repeated RAGAS evaluation tasks for the same queries (Section A.1). Metrics. End-to-end generation runs report faithfulness and answer relevance (RAGAS v0.4 (Es et al., 2024) judged by GPT-5.1); NDCG@10, exact match, token-level F1, and p50/p95 latency and $/query; GPT-5.1 also generates answers for all configurations. NDCG@10 follows the BEIR convention (Thakur et al., 2021): retrieved chunks are de-duplicated by parent document ID before scoring, so the metric matches the document-level qrel grain. two-annotator human evaluation validates RAGAS faithfulness (Sections C.4 and C.5 and Table 29), and two-judge sensitivity analysis (GPT-5.1 vs. Claude Sonnet 4.5) shows that judge choice shifts absolute faithfulness but preserves profile ranking, so we treat single-judge point estimates as approximate and rely on ordinal comparisons for all headline claims (Section F.7). third-judge robustness check asks Claude Opus 4.7 to score 220 question-answer-context examples using the same scoring instructions (Section F.8). Its moderate agreement with the primary judge (Pearson r=0.44, Cohens κ=0.35) supports the same conclusion: relative trends persist, although exact faithfulness scores depend on the judge. Metric definitions and judge-bias mitigations in Section C.1. Pre-declared hypotheses. Most published RAG ablations tune one component at time on single benchmark at 50K corpus, and report the resulting gain as recommended configuration. We pre-declared (van Miltenburg et al., 2021; Forde & Paganini, 2019) three hypotheses that together test whether this methodology is sound, by asking whether RAG pipelines can be designed compositionally: H1 tests additivity (the assumption behind isolated single-component ablations), H2 tests profile generality (the assumption that single balanced recipe deploys across targets), and H3 tests scale invariance (the assumption that rankings measured on small corpora persist at larger corpus scales). The full pre-registration (operational definitions, statistical thresholds, exclusion criteria, post-hoc corrections) is reproduced in Section A.2. H1 Components do not necessarily combine additively. H1 tests whether two-way interactions among the eight experimental dimensions explain at least 20% of faithfulness variance. If they do, gains measured in isolation cannot be assumed to persist when components are combined. H2 single RAG composition can span multiple deployment targets. RAG designs face Pareto tradeoff: retrieval quality, faithfulness, and response time cannot be maximized jointly,

Rejecting H2 means each deployment must hand-tune its own operating point (formalism and correction: Section A.2). H3 Composition rankings shift with corpus scale. Confirming H3 means small-corpus benchmarks are methodologically suspect as scale-invariant selectors of RAG designs; rejecting it validates them as predictive across the scales tested (per-composition log-linear fits, slope-range threshold, bootstrap CIs, and Kendalls τ rank-flip test in Section A.2).

sections.title: 5 RESULTS
sections.content: H1: the benefit of RAG technique depends on the complete RAG pipeline and the target metric. Across the factorial and targeted tests, some techniques reinforce one another, some add roughly as expected, and others overlap or interfere  (Fig. 3)  . Thus, improvements measured by changing one pipeline stage at time do not reliably add up in complete RAG pipeline. We quantify this by comparing the gain predicted from separately measured improvements with the gain the combined pipeline actually delivers. This needs only the configurations the study already runs, whereas estimating all 28 pairwise interactions directly requires 232 parameters, more than design of this size can support (Section D.3). The three largest separately measured retrieval gains, from cross-encoder reranking, disabling MMR, and document-awareness prefixes, predict +46.6% lift over the DEFAULT_STANDARD baseline (NDCG@10 = 0.412; Table 32). On this same split BM25-only retriever scores 0.403 and recommended off-the-shelf dense encoder 0.436  (Table 60)  , so this is realistic starting point, not weak one. The BALANCED pipeline, which combines these techniques, realizes only +17.2%, 63% shortfall relative to the three-technique prediction. Including all five separately positive retrieval techniques raises the shortfall to 72%  (Fig. 9)  ; across 17 tested combinations, it ranges from 7% to 72%, with median of 41% (Sections D.12 and D.14). The ablations suggest partial functional overlap: reranking already provides some of the filtering benefit obtained by disabling MMR, leaving less room for the two techniques to help when combined. The target metric matters as well: embedding, enrichment, and reranking dominate the retrieval-quality metric, whereas query augmentation and agentic gating dominate the answer-faithfulness metric, which measures whether generated claims are supported by the retrieved context. Across matched pipeline configurations, the two metrics are essentially unrelated (Fig. 7; pooled Pearson = 0.01, = 0.91): 5% of configurations combine high faithfulness with low retrieval quality, and 6% show high retrieval quality with low faithfulness. The same near-zero relationship appears when each benchmark is examined separately, removing the concern that the near-zero correlation is caused by pooling benchmarks (Section D.2). This indicates that RAG pipeline selection must evaluate both metrics: selecting pipeline based only on the retrieval metric can yield strong retrieval but weakly grounded answers, while selecting one based only on the faithfulness metric can hide poor retrieval. H1: retrieval quality is most strongly associated with embedding and enrichment. On the retrieval track (Fig. 3, upper triangle; n=167 configurations), the largest marginal associations are embedding (η2 = 0.164), enrichment (η2 = 0.144), and reranking (η2 = 0.090). These unadjusted values are used for exploratory screening and are not additive because the D-optimal design is unbalanced and the effects share variance. Compression and agentic gate contribute negligibly (η2 < 0.01 each). Two two-way interactions survive both Bonferroni and BenjaminiHochberg FDR correction: Embedding Enrichment (η2 = 0.102) and Embedding Reranking (η2 = 0.110). Both survivors involve the embedding model. We attribute Embedding Enrichment to representation capacity: stronger embedders can encode added context without diluting the original passage. We attribute Embedding Reranking to candidate-set quality: rerankers have less room to help when the initial embedding already retrieves strong candidates (Sections J.3.1 and J.3.2). MMR reduces NDCG@10 by 3.6% relative on average, opposite its usual benefit on broad, heterogeneous corpora  (Table 44)  . NDCG@10 across six corpus sizes separates into two regimes (Fig. 4a): SPEED and STANDARD degrade log-linearly, while BALANCED and MAX-RELIABLE are approximately flat. The regimes cross between 15K and 25K. STANDARD leads at the small sizes (5K, 15K); BALANCED leads from 25K onward. At 200K, BALANCED exceeds STANDARD by 13.7% relative (p = 0.003; full per-size table in Section E.1). We attribute the flatter retrieval-NDCG degradation at scale of BALANCED to several retrieval-stage additions relative to STANDARD: broader chunk retention, hierarchical document partitioning, and post-retrieval merging (full list in Section I.1). Together, these sustain denser, higher-signal top-k as distractors dilute the pool. The extractive compression and document-awareness prefixes that BALANCED additionally enables act post-retrieval and pre-generation respectively; they primarily support faithfulness rather than the NDCG@10 gap (Section D.12; examples in document awareness and the 50K crossover). SPEED degrades fastest, which we hypothesize reflects MiniLM-L6s limited discriminative capacity (384-dim) operating without the lexical anchoring that BM25 would provide under hybrid retrieval, see example and Table 23 for results. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We study how modern RAG techniques compose across pipeline stages, metrics, and corpus scales using LASAGNA, stage-isolated framework, and 450 configurations across eight benchmarks from 5K to 200K documents. Gains measured one component at time do not necessarily persist in complete pipelines; retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor different choices; and the best composition changes with corpus scale. New techniques should be tested in representative complete pipelines, on both metrics, and at the intended scale. We release LASAGNA to make such studies practical and reproducible, and to establish compositional evaluation as the reporting standard for new RAG techniques rather than the isolated single-component ablations common today. sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: LASAGNA is an evaluation framework operating over publicly released retrieval benchmarks; no human subjects, personal data, or private corpora were used. LLM API calls totalled approximately $5,200 and 310 wall-clock hours (Section A.7); we report per-configuration cost and latency to enable reproducibility on constrained budgets. Because the framework lowers the cost of composing RAG pipelines, users deploying it in domain applications requiring corpus-specific validation should re-validate our profile candidates on their own corpus before deployment. Our headline profile comparisons rest on one constructed English multi-domain test bed with 93 retrieval and 200 generation queries per experiment, so the profiles are best interpreted as candidates for further validation, not prescriptions. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT The LASAGNA framework code is released at https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna. The paperspecific artifacts cited by path in the appendices (the D-optimal design matrix, per-configuration profiles, per-query raw scores, and analysis scripts) are not part of that release and are available from the authors on request. Sections to document experimental design and pre-registration; the perexperiment provenance manifest  (Table 58)  , conformance test verifying stage isolation (Section H.1), and full compute accounting (Section A.7) support end-to-end reproducibility. The design matrix, hypotheses, and decision rules were pre-declared internally and hashed (SHA-256) prior to execution; we did not file third-party timestamped pre-registration (OSF/AsPredicted), so the main text says pre-declared rather than pre-registered.

sections.title: LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Our evaluation uses one constructed English multi-domain test bed ( 93 retrieval queries, 200 generation queries per experiment) and does not test: multilingual corpora, real enterprise or private data, open-weight generators (all headline results use proprietary APIs; see Reproducibility Statement), or cross-organizational large corpora. Faithfulness is now measured under two generator models rather than one (Section F.9), which is sensitivity check on generator choice and not sweep: both models are proprietary, and the ordering of the two closest profiles is not stable across them. Findings should be interpreted as case-study evidence for the methodological framework, and derived profiles as candidates for further validation rather than prescriptions for high-stakes deployments. On the evaluation side, our cross-judge (LLM and humans) agreement supports profile rankings across LLM judges, but absolute faithfulness scores still live in single judges calibration. sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Summary of the pre-registration. In one sentence: we commit, before collecting data, to testing whether practitioner can build good Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline by tuning components one at time on small corpus, the way the literature implicitly assumes. The study commits to three confirmatory hypotheses (Section A.2.2), 242-configuration D-optimal fractional factorial design spanning 8 pipeline dimensions, 5 benchmark datasets (2,300 queries per configuration), and three-track evaluation protocol covering retrieval, end-to-end generation, and hallucination resistance. To our knowledge, this is the first pre-declared factorial evaluation of RAG pipeline composition, 4.6 the scale of the largest prior controlled RAG study (Jin et al., 2025). We publish this document before experimental data collection to establish hypothesis commitment and invite community feedback on model selection, benchmark composition, and statistical methodology. A.2.1 MOTIVATION AND RATIONALE Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al., 2020) has become the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external knowledge. rich toolkit of individually validated techniques, dense retrieval, hybrid sparsedense fusion, cross-encoder reranking, HyDE (Gao et al., 2023a), CRAG (Yan et al., 2024), Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024), is available to practitioners, yet each technique is evaluated in isolation against simple baseline. Practitioners who combine several techniques simultaneously have no empirical basis for predicting whether their gains add, cancel, or amplify. This is not merely reporting gap. Wang et al. (2024) observe that end-to-end RAG performance depends on coordinated pipeline design rather than any single component; Chen et al. (2026) confirm the presence of interaction effects by showing that jointly optimized RAG components outperform independently tuned ones. Yet neither work measures the sign, magnitude, or domain-dependence of these interactions under controlled factorial conditions, precisely the question practitioner faces when choosing configuration for production. Pre-registration prevents post-hoc hypothesis mining, known problem in ML benchmarking (Dodge et al., 2019; Bouthillier et al., 2021). By committing to hypotheses, analysis plans, and exclusion criteria before data collection, we ensure that our confirmatory findings are distinguishable from exploratory ones. We additionally publish this document to invite community input on experimental choices that remain open (Section A.2.3). A.2.2 PRE-REGISTERED HYPOTHESES We pre-register three hypotheses that together ask whether RAG pipelines can be designed compositionally. H1 asks the structural question: do the eight pipeline components combine additively, or do they interact non-trivially? If they interact, the implicit assumption behind every single-component ablation in the literature fails. H2 asks the design question: assuming components do interact, can single fixed configuration still serve practitioners across the (faithfulness, latency, cost) tradeoff space, or must each deployment hand-tune for its own operating point? H3 asks the scaling question: do the answers to H1 and H2 survive 40 scale-up of the corpus, or are small-corpus best practices misleading at production scale? sections.content: Pre-registered claim. Two-way interactions between the eight factorial dimensions explain 20% of the variance in faithfulness (RAGAS, 01 scale) after main effects are removed. Variance is reported as partial η2, the share of residual variance (after main effects) attributed to interaction terms, in Type-III ANOVA, an ANOVA decomposition that estimates each terms contribution after partialling out all others and is robust to unbalanced designs. The pre-registered 20% bar is stricter than Cohens conventional large effect reference of η2 partial 0.14 (Cohen, 2013). Pre-registered test. F-test on the joint set of all 28 two-way interaction terms, α = 0.05. Post-hoc Bonferroni (α = 0.05/28 = 0.00179) per interaction pair. What confirming and rejecting mean. Confirming H1 falsifies the additivity assumption behind most single-component RAG ablations in the literature: designer cannot tune one component in isolation and trust the gain to compose with another. Rejecting H1 (interaction terms contribute <5% of variance) means RAG components are approximately additive within the precision of our 242-config sweep, and isolated ablations remain defensible practice. H2, balanced operating point exists. Research question. Given that components interact, can single fixed configuration sweep wider region of the (faithfulness, latency, cost) tradeoff space than quality-only configuration, or must practitioners give up an axis to gain another? Pre-registered claim. The BALANCED operational profile exhibits strictly higher hypervolume indicator (HV) than the MAX-RELIABLE profile on 3 of the 5 benchmark datasets. Hypervolume is the multi-objective generalization of area-under-the-curve: the volume of the (faithfulness, latency, cost) region dominated by the profiles per-query tradeoff cloud, with larger meaning better envelope. Pre-registered test. Wilcoxon signed-rank, non-parametric paired-sample test that does not assume normality, on per-query faithfulness scores (paired by query), Bonferroni-corrected across the 5 datasets (α = 0.05/5 = 0.01 per dataset). HV is computed with the exact 3D algorithm; objectives are normalized to [0, 1] before the volume integration. What confirming and rejecting mean. Confirming H2 says single fixed configuration can serve practitioners who do not want to give up an axis: published profile recipes (e.g., BALANCED) generalize across deployments. Rejecting H2 (MAX-RELIABLE dominates in 4/5 datasets) means production RAG requires per-deployment tuning to its own tradeoff preference, and our published profile recipes will not generalize. H3, Profile rankings flip with corpus scale. Research question. Does the best-performing RAG profile at small corpus (where most published RAG ablations live) remain the best-performing profile at production scale, or do profile rankings change with corpus size? Pre-registered claim. Fitting NDCG@10 as power law NDCG@10(N ) = aN separately for each of the four operational profiles (SPEED, STANDARD, BALANCED, MAX-RELIABLE), the cross-profile range bmax bmin exceeds 0.05 per decade of corpus growth (i.e., the steepestand shallowestdegrading profiles differ by at least 5% relative NDCG@10 per 10 corpus increase), analogous to the saturation behavior observed in neural scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020). Equivalently, the profile-rank ordering at the smallest tested corpus (5K) differs from the ordering at 200K on 1 benchmark. Pre-registered test. Per-profile nonlinear least-squares fit (scipy.optimize.curve_fit); 95% bootstrap CIs on each from 10,000 resamples. Profile-pair slope differences tested via permutation test (10,000 shuffles, α = 0.05) , non-parametric significance test that constructs the null distribution by random label shuffling, valid without distributional assumptions. Profile-rank stability tested via Kendalls τ between the 5K and 200K profile orderings. What confirming and rejecting mean. Confirming H3 means small-corpus ablations cannot reliably predict production-scale deployment choices: profile selection requires re-validation at the deployments target corpus size, and the fields reliance on 50K-corpus benchmarks is methodologically suspect for deployment decisions. Rejecting H3 (slope range 0.02 per decade, τ = 1 on every benchmark) means small-corpus benchmarks generalize, and the small-corpus best practice is also the large-corpus best practice.

DATASETS, CORPORA, AND EVALUATION PROTOCOL B.1 EVALUATION DATASET DESIGN We designed three-track evaluation protocol that separates retrieval quality measurement from generation quality measurement and hallucination resistance testing. Each track uses purpose-built corpus to ensure that the measured outcome reflects the intended evaluation dimension. Sampling strategy. Each configuration is evaluated on 149 non-overlapping queries: 93 for retrieval (stratified across 5 BEIR domains) and 56 for generation (stratified across 3 QA benchmarks). These representative subsets were drawn via stratified random sampling from the full benchmark pools (which collectively contain thousands of queries) to balance domain coverage and difficulty distribution against the $4,700 compute budget required for factorial-scale evaluation (167 configurations 149 queries = 24,883 retrieval evaluations plus 6,832 generation evaluations). The sampling preserves the original difficulty and domain distributions: each BEIR domain contributes 1122 retrieval queries proportional to its test-set size, and each QA benchmark contributes 1323 generation queries proportional to its eval-set size. While larger query sets would reduce per-configuration variance, the factorial design compensates by aggregating signal across 167 independent configurations, yielding 71,643 total evaluations, sufficient for main-effect and targeted-interaction testing at 80% power for η2 0.03 (Section 5). B.1.1 TRACK OVERVIEW Table 15 summarizes the three evaluation tracks. Tracks 1 and 2 share common base corpus; Track 2 augments it with gold passages so the retriever can surface ground-truth evidence, while Track 3 deliberately withholds gold passages to test grounding under adversarial conditions. We drew documents from five BEIR domain subsets: NFCORPUS, FIQA, SCIFACT, ARGUANA, and HOTPOTQA. These subsets span biomedical, financial, scientific, argumentative, and multi-hop reasoning domains, providing heterogeneous retrieval challenges. Distractor documents. For each benchmark we sampled 500 distractor documents from held-out BEIR collections that do not overlap with the benchmarks relevance judgments. Distractors increase corpus size and dilute signal, making retrieval metrics more discriminative. Gold passage extraction. For the end-to-end generation track (Track 2), we extracted context passages from each QA sample by splitting on double newlines (nn). Each extracted passage was assigned document identifier of the form gold:{benchmark}:{sample_id}:{passage_idx} and ingested alongside the base corpus. With 500 distractors per benchmark, gold passages represent roughly 8% of the Track 2 corpus; this ratio is substantially lower than the 84% we observed in early pilots that used only 100 distractors, yielding more realistic retrieval challenge.

Right: the E2E generation track embeds QA pairs from three reading-comprehension and multi-hop benchmarks (SQuAD v2, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) in the same pool, augmented with gold-passage documents to guarantee answerability. Scaling experiments (Section 5) inject up to 45,000 additional distractors from the same five domains in controlled increments. Stratified split. We partitioned all queries into 60/20/20 train/eval/test splits, stratified by source benchmark, so that each split contains proportional representation of every domain. The eval split guided iterative development; the test split was reserved for final reporting. B.1.3 DESIGN RATIONALE We separate the three tracks for the following reasons: 1. Retrieval track. Standard IR evaluation with BEIR relevance judgments, independent of the generation model. This isolates retrieval quality from downstream answer quality and allows direct comparison with published BEIR baselines. 2. E2E generation track. Tests the full pipeline, including answer generation. Gold passages are present in the corpus so that the retriever can find them; failure to produce correct answer therefore reflects pipeline limitations rather than corpus gaps. 3. Hallucination track. Tests whether the system hallucinates when gold evidence is absent from the corpus. faithful system should abstain or hedge rather than fabricate an answer. By reusing the same queries as Track 2 but withholding gold passages, we can attribute faithfulness differences to corpus composition rather than query difficulty. sections.content: B.2.5 ADAPTER ARCHITECTURE Benchmarks are integrated through pluggable adapter pattern  (Fig. 5)  . Each adapter implements three methods: load_queries(), load_corpus(), and load_qrels(). Two concrete adapter families exist: 1. BEIR adapter: Wraps the public BEIR download and loading utilities. Adding new BEIR dataset requires only specifying the dataset name; the adapter handles download, caching, and format normalization automatically. 2. PrivateEvalAdapter: Loads proprietary or custom datasets from local JSONL files. We use this adapter for our curated evaluation corpus (Section B.1). Adding support for new benchmark typically requires approximately 50 lines of adapter code. Third-party adapters can be registered via Python entry points (lasagna_benchmarks group) for automatic discovery. B.2.6 DATASET LICENSING All BEIR datasets are publicly available under their respective licenses (see the BEIR repository for per-dataset details). QA datasets (SQuAD, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, TriviaQA, Natural Questions) are used under their original academic licenses. BamBoogle is released under CC BY 4.0. FEVER is released under CC BY-SA 3.0. We do not redistribute any dataset; our evaluation SDK downloads them on demand from their canonical sources. B.3.5 DISTRACTOR-RELEVANCE AUDIT We audit the assumption underlying H3 that documents added to the corpus purely on the basis of doc_id disjointness from evaluation qrels are, in fact, non-relevant to the evaluation queries. This is the caveat flagged in Section 5: because distractors are drawn from the same five BEIR domains as the base corpus, fraction may be plausibly on-topic for specific query and should be re-graded as false negatives in the qrels rather than as distractors. Sample and design. We drew n=100 (distractor-document, query) pairs stratified across the five BEIR sub-benchmarks used in the scaling extension (NFCorpus, FiQA, SciFact, ArguAna, HotpotQA), 20 distractors per benchmark, paired 50/50 with either (i) that distractors top-BM25 matching query from retrieval_test.jsonl (the adversarial arm, which is most likely to surface false negative) or (ii) random query from the same query pool (the baseline arm). The distractor pool (n=2,500) is the subset of the 5,132-document corpus that is not present in the union of expected_docs across the retrieval train, eval, and test splits (union of positives = 2,840), sampled deterministically after stratification. Each pair was scored by single LLM auditor (Claude, first-pass) into {RELEVANT, PARTIALLY RELEVANT, NOT RELEVANT}. Results. Table 21 summarizes the 100-pair labeling.

C.1.3 LLM-JUDGED METRICS All LLM-judged metrics use RAGAS v0.4 (Es et al., 2024) with GPT-5.1 as the judge model at temperature =0, greedy decoding, and deterministic seed. This applies uniformly to all experiments: profile comparisons, scaling experiments, and the 122-configuration faithfulness factorial. LASAGNA wraps the RAGAS framework so the same judge configuration is reused across faithfulness, answer relevance, and context recall, and so every LLM call is deterministic under the fixed seed. Faithfulness. Faithfulness measures the fraction of claims in the generated answer that are supported by the retrieved context. RAGAS decomposes the answer into atomic claims {c1, . . . , cM } using the judge LLM, then classifies each claim as supported or not supported given the context: Faithfulness = 1 (cid:88) m=1 1(cid:2)claim cm is supported by context(cid:3). (10) faithfulness score of 1.0 indicates that every atomic claim in the answer is grounded in the retrieved passages. We use concise answer prompts (one sentence) to reduce the number of atomic claims per sample, which both accelerates evaluation and reduces variance from claim decomposition. Answer Relevance. Answer relevance estimates how well the generated answer addresses the original question. RAGAS generates =3 synthetic questions from the answer, computes the cosine similarity between each synthetic question embedding and the original question embedding, and averages: Relevance = 1 (cid:88) n= cos(cid:0)e(q), e(qn)(cid:1) , (11) where e() is the embedding function and q1, . . . , qN are the synthetic questions. sections.content: Position bias. LLM judges tend to prefer the answer presented first in the prompt (Zheng et al., 2023). For all pairwise comparisons, we run each pair twice with swapped presentation order (A-B and B-A) and record win only when the preference is consistent across both orderings. Inconsistent pairs are counted as ties. Self-preference bias. Models may prefer outputs from the same model family. Because both answer generation (GPT-5.1) and judging (GPT-5.1) use the same model, self-preference bias is concern. We mitigate this in two ways: (i) the judge evaluates answer pairs from different pipeline configurations, not from different base models, so both candidates are GPT-5.1 outputs and selfpreference does not favor either candidate; (ii) we validate 50-query subsample using Claude Sonnet 4.5 as an alternative judge to measure inter-judge agreement. We ran 80 matched samples (40 per configuration) through both judges. Kendalls τb = 0.38 (p < 0.001), Spearman ρ = 0.42 (p < 0.001), and 66% of per-sample faithfulness scores agree within 0.1 absolute points. GPT-5.1 assigns slightly higher mean faithfulness (0.879 vs. 0.860 for Claude Sonnet 4.5). This moderate, statistically significant agreement indicates that per-sample faithfulness scores are largely consistent across judge models on the two configurations sampled, though absolute scores show provider-specific calibration differences; see Section C.5 for separate pairwise-BTL protocol study showing that fine-grained configuration-level rankings are protocol-dependent while profile-tier separations are preserved. Determinism. We fix the judge model to GPT-5.1 with temperature =0 and fixed random seed across all experiments. All RAGAS evaluations use batch_size=4 to avoid rate-limit-induced timeouts, and we use paired statistical tests (paired bootstrap or Wilcoxon signed-rank, paired by query) so that any residual judge noise cancels across configurations being compared. Multiple-comparisons posture. We apply HolmBonferroni within each test family (H1 per-pair uses the pre-registered per-pair Bonferroni α/28; H3 scaling crossover uses Holm across 4 corpus sizes; H2 is single Wilcoxon test with no family). global correction across all families in Table 36 would be inappropriate because the tested hypotheses are logically independent (interaction structure vs. scaling crossover vs. Pareto dominance) and would over-inflate Type II error on the pre-registered H1 test. This appendix asks whether the profile-level conclusions survive replacing it. What varies, and what is held fixed. For each of the four profiles we reuse the documents that profile had already retrieved, so retrieval is untouched and no pipeline is re-run. We hold the answer prompt, the RAGAS judge, and the decoding temperature (T =0) fixed, and change only the model that writes the answer: GPT-5.1 (generator A, the generator used throughout the paper) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (generator B). The design is 43 questions 4 profiles 3 seeds per arm, giving 510 paired comparisons. One common answer prompt is applied to all four profiles in both arms, so the absolute values below are not commensurable with Table 2, which reports each profile under its own deployment-native prompt. sections.content: H.1 PLATFORM ISOLATION VERIFICATION To empirically validate LASAGNAs stage-isolation guarantees (Section 3), we ran five automated tests targeting the isolation properties that are critical for valid factorial comparisons. Table 63 reports the results. Table 63: Platform isolation verification results. All five tests pass, confirming that toggling one pipeline component does not silently affect anothers behavior. Test What it verifies Pydantic type enforcement Session config isolation Embedding dim detection Chunker statelessness Plugin auto-discovery Stage boundaries reject invalid types Changing session As config leaves session unchanged 384-dim vectors into 1024-dim collection raises error No cross-document state leakage between calls New backends register via decorator without code changes Result Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass The most critical test is session config isolation: we created two sessions with opposite HyDE settings (enable_hyde=True vs. False), then verified that querying the session provider returns the correct config for each session independently. In naive pipeline without session-level isolation, toggling HyDE for one experimental configuration could leak into the next, introducing confound that invalidates the factorial comparison. The embedding dimension detection test was additionally verified during the scaling experiments, where the Speed profile (MiniLM-L6, 384-dim) correctly raised EMBEDDING DIMENSION MISMATCH DETECTED when attempting to share collection with BGE-M3 (1024-dim) profiles, forcing separate ingestion, confound that would otherwise silently corrupt retrieval results. H.2 PLATFORM SHOWCASE This appendix demonstrates LASAGNAs practical usability through code examples drawn directly from the released codebase. We highlight five capabilities that distinguish the platform from existing RAG toolkits: (i) configuration UI for interactive exploration, (ii) layered plugin architecture with decorator-based registration, (iii) bring-your-own vector database support, (iv) bring-your-own agentic pipeline, and (v) agent integration via MCP. All examples are executable as shipped. H.2.1 CONFIGURATION UI LASAGNA ships three browser-based interfaces. The centerpiece is the RAG Configurator (Figs. 12 and 13), profile-centric pipeline builder that lets practitioner assemble working configuration without writing code or YAML. The left-hand rail lists the four built-in profiles (DEFAULT, SPEED, STANDARD, BALANCED, MAX-RELIABLE) alongside user-saved custom profiles, and the main panel groups every configuration key exposed by the SDK into four tabs, Essential, Search & Retrieval, Processing, and Advanced, each labeled with plain-language explanations of what the setting does, its cost implications, and the underlying YAML key (e.g. enable_hybrid_search, enable_reranking, use_agentic_rag). Every change is import/export-round-trippable with the YAML contract used by the evaluation SDK (Section H.2.5), so user can prototype profile in the UI, export it, and run

The Configurator is what gives researchers and practitioners who are not fluent in the 127-key configuration surface direct path to reproducing the operational profiles in Section 5 and to iterating on them. The other two interfaces are complementary but are not part of the public release. The Agentic Chat workspace provides conversational front-end with inline document management and citation rendering; it consumes Configurator-produced profile and lets changes take effect on the next query without restarting the server. The RAG Dashboard is evaluation-oriented, with six pages (Overview, Explorer, Impact, Pareto, Benchmark, Timeline) that visualize per-query evaluation scores. In particular: (i) the MMR finding (disable MMR) may not hold for corpora with genuinely redundant documents; (ii) the corpus-size threshold of 25K is approximate and domain-dependent; (iii) absolute latency values depend on infrastructure and will differ from our measurements. Decision rule for borderline cases (OFAT vs. hierarchical disagreement). Several configuration comparisons in this paper differ in rank order depending on whether the reader uses the OFAT (pooled) reading or the hierarchical mixed-effects (query-clustered) reading. When the two disagree by 1 rank position, defer to the hierarchical reading. It respects the query-clustering structure (ICC=0.284 on the H1 D5D8 grid; see Section D.3) and is our primary inferential position throughout the paper. The archetypal case is the H1 D5D8 attenuation: the OFAT estimate is η2=0.201 (p=0.018 Holm) whereas the hierarchical LRT is χ2(4)=4.27, p=0.371. The same pair reads as large exploratory interaction under OFAT and as non-significant under hierarchical inference. The only exception is when deployments per-query variance is orthogonal to query-topic clustering (rare in practice for benchmark corpora but possible in enterprise deployments with strictly independent queries); in that regime the pooled OFAT reading is closer to the deployment target. separate, orthogonal protocol-dependence axis (point-wise RAGAS-judge vs. pairwise BradleyTerry) affects within-tier configuration comparisons; see Section C.5 for the tier-vs-configuration scoping. sections.content: Performance. Lowest retrieval NDCG@10 across SOTA profiles (0.415 at 5K; degrades to 0.382 at 15K).2 The underlying speed profile achieves the highest mean faithfulness (0.980, median 1.000) in deployment evaluations (Section I.3); SOTA_SPEED shares the same retrieval configuration and thus the same faithfulness characteristics. Dominant p95 latency: 200 ms retrieval, 800 ms end-to-end. Success root causes. 1. Pipeline simplicity as implicit noise filter. With only 10 dense-retrieved chunks and no postprocessing, the generator receives clean, unmodified context window. The absence of MMR (R2), reranking reordering, and compression means the generator sees passages in their original embedding-similarity order, which empirically correlates with higher faithfulness (Table 46: speed achieves 0.991 on scifact). This aligns with findings that simpler retrieval pipelines produce fewer hallucinations because the generator has less opportunity to be confused by reordered or deduplicated context (Liu et al., 2024). Note that the speed profile does not use document awareness (G3), its faithfulness advantage is entirely attributable to pipeline simplicity, not to generation-side features. 2. Concise generation prompting. The speed profile uses concise answer prompt (Answer in ONE sentence based only on the context), which limits the number of atomic claims per answer. Fewer claims mean fewer opportunities for unsupported statements, mechanically improving RAGAS faithfulness (Es et al., 2024). This is measurement artifact as much as genuine quality improvement: one-sentence answer with one correct claim scores higher than three-sentence answer with two correct claims and one hallucinated claim. Failure root causes. 1. Embedding capacity ceiling. MiniLM-L6 (384d, 22M parameters) has fundamentally lower representational capacity than BGE-M3 (1024d, 568M parameters). The factorial ANOVA confirms embedding choice as the strongest main effect on NDCG@10 (η2 = 0.164, < 0.001; Section 5). On nfcorpus (biomedical), the capacity gap manifests as 0.050 NDCG@10 versus SOTA balanced  (Table 45)  . 2. No lexical fallback (R5 absent). Dense-only retrieval (α=1.0) has no BM25 component to capture exact entity matches. The hybrid ablation (Exp. 01) shows that adding BM25 at α=0.5 yields +0.037 NDCG@10, gain entirely unavailable to this profile. 3. Rapid scaling degradation (C3). Speed degrades at 0.115 NDCG/decade (R2 = 0.900, 95% CI [0.168, 0.062]), the steepest slope of any profile  (Table 23)  . Without hybrid search to provide lexical anchoring, dense retrieval quality deteriorates rapidly as distractor density increases. sections.content: Assessment. The speed profile is well-calibrated for its stated purpose (sub-second latency) but exhibits fundamental retrieval ceiling that makes it unsuitable when NDCG@10 > 0.5 is required. Its faithfulness advantage is partially artifactual (concise prompting reduces claim surface) and should not be interpreted as genuine superiority in answer quality. J.2.2 SOTA_STANDARD: RETRIEVAL CHAMPION, SCALE-FRAGILE Configuration summary. BGE-M3 (1024d), hybrid search (α=0.5), cross-encoder reranking (mxbai-rerank-large-v1, top-5), HyDE (3 variants), no MMR, direct generation route (query routing disabled, standard tier default) with the hallucination and answer-quality gates enabled at the pipeline level, top-k=20 (Section I.1.2). Performance. Highest NDCG@10 at small scale (0.510 at 5K; 0.860 on E2E at 5.5K). Degrades to 0.456 at 50K and 0.432 at 200K, overtaken by balanced, with the gap becoming statistically significant only at 200K ( = +0.059, = 0.004). Faithfulness: 0.739 (E2E, 5.5K), lower than all other SOTA profiles except Max-Reliable at scale. Success root causes. 1. Optimal retrieval stack for small corpora. The standard profile combines four high-impact retrieval features: (a) cross-encoder reranking (which our ablation shows adds up to +0.084 NDCG@10 with the best model, ms-marco-MiniLM-L6; the default mxbai-large used by standard provides smaller gain, see failure analysis below); (b) hybrid search (+0.037; R5 exploited); (c) MMR disabled (+0.046; R2 avoided); (d) HyDE (+0.026; R4). Despite the suboptimal reranker choice, the four features jointly lift the profile to 0.510 NDCG@10 at 5K, the highest retrieval score among SOTA profiles, confirming that the retrieval stack is well-chosen even if individual components are not individually optimal (Section D.1). 2. HyDE as bridging context (R4 positive mode). HyDE generates hypothetical documents that bridge the vocabulary gap between short queries and long passages. On hotpotqa (multi-hop), the standard profile achieves +0.088 NDCG@10 over the baseline  (Table 45)  , consistent with HyDEs demonstrated effectiveness on multi-hop queries (Gao et al., 2023a). The cross-encoder reranker acts as noise filter for HyDEs occasionally hallucinated passages, preventing degradation (R4 positive mode in the taxonomy). Failure root causes. 1. Reranker model suboptimality (R1). The standard profile uses mxbai-rerank-large-v1, which our reranker model ablation (Exp. 15) identified as underperforming the smaller specialist msmarco-MiniLM-L6 on the shared 93-query retrieval-isolation benchmark (NDCG@10 = 0.470 vs 0.496, 0.026 gap; Table 51). The SOTA evaluation configs retain mxbai-large because it was the framework default and the profile configs were frozen before the reranker comparison was conducted. Note that the reranker is query-time knob (not in _INGESTION_TIME_KEYS; experiment.py:6087), so re-running with the swapped reranker requires no re-ingestion of the corpus. The isolated model-swap delta (+0.026; Table 51) shrinks to +0.009 NDCG@10 when measured end-to-end on the BEIR generation split with the full SOTA_Std stack composed  (Table 59)  , consistent with functional-duplication interactions (C1). The swap remains the single easiest available improvement for the standard profile. 2. Scale fragility (C3). The standard profile degrades log-linearly at 0.055 NDCG/decade (R2 = 0.895, = 0.004), 3.7 steeper slope than balanced (0.015/decade; slope not distinguishable from zero, = 0.175; Table 23). The root cause is the absence of generation-side defenses: without context compression (G2) or document awareness (G3), the generator receives 5 fulllength passages (up to 4,000 tokens) whose relevance quality degrades as corpus size increases. At 50K documents, the proportion of near-miss distractors in the top-20 candidate set increases, and without compression to distil the most relevant spans, the generator is more likely to attend to irrelevant context. This mechanism is consistent with the lost in the middle phenomenon (Liu et al., 2024), where generators struggle to utilize relevant information when it is embedded in long, partially irrelevant context window. 3. No faithfulness safeguards. The standard profile achieves the lowest faithfulness among SOTA profiles (0.739 at 5.5K; Table 2). Without agentic quality gates (G1), hallucination checks, or context compression (G2), the generator operates on raw retrieved context with no verification

On the joint retrievalfaithfulnesslatency hypervolume, STANDARD has the highest HV at the fixed 30 reference  (Table 2)  and BALANCED takes over once Lref opens past 46 (e.g., HV=0.609 vs STANDARDs 0.579 at 60 s; Table 39). NDCG@10: 0.504 at 5K, 0.488 at 50K, 0.491 at 200K, effectively flat (0.015/decade, R2 = 0.40, slope not distinguishable from zero, = 0.175). Overtakes STANDARD on the retrieval track with statistically significant margin at 200K (p = 0.004). Faithfulness on the SOTA-profile headline slice: 0.911 0.014. Mean latency: 12.3 (p95 17.726.3 across measurements). Success root causes. 1. Retrieval foundation partially shared with STANDARD, with retrieval-visible additions. BALANCED and STANDARD share embedding model (BAAI/bge-m3), reranker (mxbai-large), hybrid alpha, MMR settings, chunker parameters, and top-k; BALANCED additionally enables hierarchical parent/child indexing (index-stage), structured-graph post-retrieval merge, wider chunk-cite keep count (max_chunks = 20 vs. 15 for STANDARD), and adaptive query routing. These four retrieval-visible additions, rather than the compression or document-awareness features

sections.content: below, drive the small-scale retrieval parity (0.504 vs. 0.510; = 0.006, within noise) and the widening gap at scale. 2. Context compression as generation-side noise filter (G2). Extractive compression at 50% ratio removes filler tokens from retrieved passages while preserving the most relevant spans, acting post-retrieval on chunk text (chunks are not reordered or dropped by this step). The generator receives denser, higher-signal context window, reducing the lost in the middle failure mode and lowering the token budget available for hallucination, improving faithfulness ( = +0.01; Section D.1). The dropout analysis reports small 0.006 NDCG@10 delta when compression is removed (Section D.12); this reflects the pipelines final SearchResult list being scored, not compression modifying retrieval ordering per se. 3. Document awareness as cheap grounding (G3). The 100-token document prefix provides file-level metadata (filename, structure, opening sentences) at negligible cost (+15 ms latency). Exp. 17 (eval split, exploratory) demonstrates that this simple strategy outperforms LLM-generated summaries (0.411 vs. 0.341 NDCG@10) and longer prefixes (300 tokens: 0.347). The mechanism is information-theoretic: the first 100 tokens of document contain high-entropy information (title, abstract, introduction) that helps the generator contextualize retrieved chunks. Longer prefixes add boilerplate that dilutes signal. Worked Example: Document Awareness Grounds Financial Query (G3) Query (FiQA): Opening Roth IRA account, what is the fee structure for Vanguard vs. Scottrade? Without document awareness (standard profile): Top-5 reranked chunks: 3 about Vanguard fees, 2 about brokerage accounts generically Generator sees 5 passage fragments with no file-level context Generated answer discusses Vanguard fees accurately but hallucinates Scottrade fee schedule (Scottrade chunk at Rank 8, outside top-10) Faithfulness: 0.67 (one claim unsupported) With 100-token prefix (balanced profile): Each chunk is prefixed with the first 100 tokens of its source document: [Vanguard_fee_schedule.pdf] Vanguard offers several types of IRA accounts including Traditional, Roth, and SEP. . . The generator can now distinguish which document each chunk originates from and recognize that no Scottrade document is present in the context Generated answer correctly states Vanguard fees and notes that insufficient information is available for Scottrade Faithfulness: 1.00 The 100-token prefix costs only +15 ms but enables the generator to reason about source provenance, which documents are present and, critically, which are absent. Longer prefixes (300 tokens) dilute this signal with boilerplate, explaining the diminishing returns observed in Exp. 17 (0.411 at 100 tokens vs. 0.347 at 300 tokens). 4. Scale robustness from generation-side defenses (C3 mitigated). The combination of compression and document awareness provides two independent defenses against scale-induced degradation: compression filters noisy passages, and awareness provides document-level context that remains informative even when individual chunks become less relevant. The balanced profiles degradation slope (0.015 NDCG/decade, not significantly different from zero, = 0.175) is 3.7 flatter than standards (0.055, = 0.004), directly attributable to these features. On E2E faithfulness, balanced maintains 0.935 at 50K vs. standards 0.793, +0.142 gap that widens with scale. 5. Composition penalty minimized by complementary features. Unlike the Max-Reliable profile (which stacks overlapping features), balanceds additions (compression, awareness) operate on different pipeline stages than its retrieval features. Compression acts on the output of reranking (post-retrieval); awareness acts on the generation prompt (pre-generation). Neither duplicates the function of HyDE, reranking, or hybrid search. The dropout analysis (Section D.12) confirms this complementarity: removing compression from balanced costs only 0.006 NDCG@10, and removing document awareness costs 0.055, while removing the reranker costs 0.072, each features dropout delta is close to its single-feature ablation delta, indicating minimal interference. By contrast, the full five-feature stack (Section D.14) incurs 72% composition penalty precisely because retrieval-side features overlap in function. Failure root causes.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: 1. Reranker inheritance (R1). Like standard, balanced inherits the suboptimal mxbai-large reranker. The reranker model ablation (Exp. 15) shows +0.026 NDCG@10 gap between mxbai-large and the best model (ms-marco-MiniLM-L6); the actual gain from swapping in composed profile would be smaller due to interactions, but reranker selection remains the largest single opportunity. 2. HyDE profile-dependence (R4 negative mode). The dropout analysis shows that removing HyDE from balanced improves NDCG@10 by +0.008  (Table 44)  , suggesting that in this specific feature combination, HyDEs noisy hypothetical documents slightly degrade retrieval quality. The magnitude is small (< 2% relative) and the improvement is within noise, but it indicates that HyDEs benefit is not universal across profiles, clear interaction effect. Assessment. The balanced profiles strong agentic tradeoff arises from principled design: it exhausts the retrieval stack (where the largest gains are available) and adds generation-side defenses that address different failure modes (noise filtering, context grounding) rather than amplifying the same capability. This complementary design minimizes the composition penalty and provides scale robustness that retrieval-only profiles lack. J.2.4 SOTA_MAX_RELIABLE: MAXIMUM FEATURES, DIMINISHING RETURNS Configuration summary. BGE-M3 (1024d), hybrid search (α=0.3), cross-encoder reranking (mxbai-rerank-large-v1, top-5), HyDE (3 variants), no MMR, hierarchical retrieval enabled, contextual retrieval enabled, agentic generation route (3 iterations, hallucination and answer-quality gates enabled), extractive compression (50%), document awareness (100-token prefix), top-k=20, up to 30 retained chunks (Section I.1.4). Differs from BALANCED on retrieval-side choices (hybrid α, contextual retrieval, maximum retained chunks); the two configurations share the same agentic route depth and the same quality-gate set. Performance. Has weaker joint tradeoff than BALANCED within the agentic-route class at essentially equal faithfulness (0.916 vs. 0.911) with 13.5% higher mean latency (p=0.018 paired Wilcoxon on per-query latency; Table 2 and Section D.8). NDCG@10: 0.804 (E2E, 5.5K), lower than STANDARDs 0.860. Faithfulness on the SOTA-profile headline slice: 0.916 0.022. Mean latency: 14.2 (2 above BALANCED). Success root causes. 1. Hallucination gating (G1 positive mode). The agentic pipelines hallucination check filters retrieved chunks that the LLM judge classifies as not supporting the query. This raises the floor of per-query faithfulness: the minimum observed score is 0.812  (Table 65)  , compared to 0.750 for balanced and 0.714 for standard. For safety-critical deployments, raising the floor matters more than improving the mean. 2. Quality gate as safety net (G4). The quality gate evaluates the generated answer against the retrieved context and can trigger re-retrieval if the answer appears unfaithful. This multi-iteration loop provides second chance for queries where the initial retrieval was poor. The faithfulness ANOVA confirms that the Query AugmentationAgentic Gate interaction is the strongest two-way effect on faithfulness (η2 = 0.191, < 0.001; Section 5), and Max-Reliable is the only SOTA profile that activates both components. Failure root causes. 1. Aggressive refinement paradox (G1 negative mode). The agentic pipelines chunk refinement classifies 1314 of 15 retrieved chunks as not relevant on multi-hop queries, discarding evidence that the generator needs for comprehensive answers. When all chunks are discarded, single fallback chunk is returned. This starves the generator: with one chunk of 800 tokens, the answer is necessarily incomplete. The dropout analysis confirms this: removing agentic RAG from the Max-Reliable base profile improves NDCG@10 by +0.021  (Table 44)  . Separately, the cross-profile comparison shows E2E exact match at 0.163 (standard) vs. 0.101 (Max-Reliable), consistent with reduced answer completeness. Mechanistic detail. The refinement uses an LLM judge to classify each chunk as RELEVANT, PARTIALLY_RELEVANT, or NOT_RELEVANT. The judge operates on individual chunks without cross-chunk context, so chunk that provides necessary bridging evidence for multi-hop query

sections.content: may be classified as not relevant because it does not directly answer the query. This is consistent with the pointwise scoring approach used in passage reranking (Nogueira & Cho, 2019), where each passage is evaluated independently; the effect is amplified when the refinement threshold is aggressive (our default: only RELEVANT chunks pass). Worked Example: The Aggressive Refinement Paradox on Multi-Hop Query (G1) Query (MuSiQue): In what part of Florida is Tom Denneys birthplace located? This query decomposes into two hops: (1) Where was Tom Denney born? (2) What part of Florida is that city in? Retrieval (shared across balanced and Max-Reliable): top-15 chunks include: C1 Tom Denney (born 1982) is guitarist from Coral Springs, Florida. . . HOP 1: BIRTHPLACE C4 Coral Springs is city in Broward County, in the southeastern part of the state. . . HOP 2: LOCATION C7 Denney was the lead guitarist and founding member of Day to Remember. . . BIOGRAPHICAL CONTEXT C9C15 Various passages about Florida cities, other musicians from Florida DISTRACTORS Max_reliable refinement (3-iteration agentic pipeline): Iteration 1: LLM judge classifies each chunk independently against the query C1 PARTIALLY_RELEVANT (mentions birthplace but not part of Florida) C4 NOT_RELEVANT (discusses Coral Springs geography but does not mention Tom Denney) C7 NOT_RELEVANT (biography, no location info) C9C15 NOT_RELEVANT Result: 14/15 chunks discarded. Only C1 passes (downgraded from PARTIALLY_RELEVANT by the strict threshold). Fallback: 1 chunk returned. Generated answers: Balanced (all 5 reranked chunks passed to generator): Tom Denney was born in Coral Springs, which is in the southeastern part of Florida. Correct, both hops answered. Faithfulness: 1.0, EM: 1. Max_reliable (1 fallback chunk, C1 only): Tom Denney was born in Coral Springs, Florida. Partially correct, birthplace is stated but part of Florida is missing (C4 was discarded). Faithfulness: 1.0 (answer is grounded), but EM: 0 (incomplete). The paradox: Max-Reliable achieves higher faithfulness (the answer is fully grounded in the single chunk it kept) but lower answer completeness (it cannot answer the second hop). The pointwise judge cannot recognize that C4 is essential bridging evidence because C4 alone says nothing about Tom Denney. 2. Latency cost without proportional quality gain. The agentic pipeline adds 37 LLM calls per query (planning, per-chunk relevance classification, hallucination check, quality gate, optional re-retrieval). Each call adds 13 via the API gateway, contributing to the +2.0 p95 latency increase over balanced. The faithfulness gain (+0.005 over balanced) does not justify this cost for most applications, making the profile less efficient on the joint tradeoff. 3. Composition penalty from feature stacking (C1). Max_reliable activates everything that balanced has plus agentic components. But the agentic pipeline partially duplicates the function of context compression: both reduce the context to high-relevance spans. When both are active, the marginal benefit of each is reduced. The waterfall analysis (Section D.14) already shows 72% composition penalty for balanceds five-feature stack, meaning only 28% of the predicted additive improvement is realized. Adding the agentic layer on top can only increase this penalty: the dropout analysis confirms that removing agentic RAG from the Max-Reliable base profile improves NDCG@10 by +0.021  (Table 44)  , indicating that the agentic layer is net-harmful for retrieval quality when compression is already active. Max_reliables composition penalty therefore exceeds 72%, making it the most penalty-heavy SOTA profile. 4. Reranker inheritance (R1) and no query expansion benefit. Max_reliable inherits the suboptimal mxbai-large reranker (R1) and explicitly disables query expansion and RAG fusion, features that its YAML config notes add latency, no faith. gain. This is correct based on single-feature ablation (R3: query expansion hurts NDCG by 0.014), but means that the agentic pipeline receives the same retrieval input as balanced, limiting its potential for improvement to the generation side only. Assessment. Max_reliable is specialized profile whose design is optimized for raising the faithfulness floor rather than the mean. Its joint disadvantage relative to balanced is driven by the aggressive refinement paradox (G1): the same mechanism that raises the faithfulness floor also reduces answer completeness. For deployments where the minimum acceptable faithfulness is the binding
